1.
The present claim petition arises out of road accident in which one Udayveer Balmiki suffered grievous injury and amputation of left lower limb.
An application u/s 166(1) MV Act was accordingly filed by the claimant/petitioner.

2. Brief facts of the case are that on 09.01.2021 at about 05:30 p.m.,
petitioner/injured Udayveer Balmiki was travelling on his motorcycle number UP-81BJ-5840 from Agra to Kuverpur Chauraha, at a normal speed according to traffic rules.

At about 03:00 p.m. when he reached Reliance Petrol Pump, Ghhalesar,
a TSR (Chhota Hathi) bearing no.UP-83BT-7724 (hereafter referred to as the offending vehicle) came at a high speed from behind and hit the motorcycle which petitioner was riding.
Due to the impact, petitioner fell and sustained grievous injury.
He was removed to S.S. Hospital, Agra where his MLC was prepared.
Thereafter on 11.01.2021, he was referred to Pushpanjali Hospital, Agra.
He was further referred to JPN Apex Trauma Center AIIMS, New Delhi for treatment where he was operated and his left leg above knee was amputed.

sentences.text: 10. In the instant case, petitioner has deposed about the manner of his accident.
He has categorically stated that the accident occurred due to negligence of the offending vehicle which struck his motorcycle from behind.
The averment has been refuted by learned counsel for insurance company during cross- examination by putting suggestions regarding negligent driving by the petitioner himself.
Petitioner has denied the suggestions.

Though during cross-examination, petitioner has admitted that he did not have a valid driving licence at the time of accident, no evidence has been led by the insurance company or the other respondents to show in what manner the petitioner could have contributed to the accident by not possessing driving licence.

Without establishing or demonstrating that the petitioner contributed to the occurrence of the accident, mere absence of driving licence cannot be a ground to assume negligence on his part, particularly where the accident has occurred due to the offending vehicle hitting the motorcycle of the petitioner from behind.

sentences.text: . The gist of the law is that the object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

16. Further it can be noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;

16.6. Observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rajkumar v. Ajay Kumar & Anr. is quoted hereunder:
"10. Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.

The Tribunal has to first ascertain what activities the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of the permanent ability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The second step is to ascertain his avocation, profession and nature of work before the accident, as also his age.

The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood, or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions, but could carry on some other or lesser scale of activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood.
For example, if the left hand of a claimant is amputated, the permanent physical or functional disablement may be assessed around 60%.
If the claimant was a driver or a carpenter, the actual loss of earning capacity may virtually be hundred percent, if he is neither able to drive or do carpentry.

On the other hand, if the claimant was a clerk in government service, the loss of his left hand may not result in loss of employment and he may still be continued as a clerk as he could perform his clerical functions; and in that event the loss of earning capacity will not be 100% as in the case of a driver or carpenter, nor 60% which is the actual physical disability, but Uday Veer Balmiki vs Shailender Singh on 30 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/153502357/

In the present case, petitioner has relied upon disability certificate issued from Pt.
Madan Mohan Malviya Hospital, Delhi noticing permanent disability of 80% in relation to left lower limb above the knee amputation.

Petitioner has examined Ms.
Sakshi from Otto Bock Healthcare Pvt. Ltd as PW-2.
In her testimony, PW-2 has stated that by implanting an artificial limb, petitioner would be able to do his daily routine work but may not be able to do rigorous work.
In these circumstances, the functional disability of the petitioner would be much less than the disability assessed without an artificial limb.

This is particularly so as the petitioner cannot be allowed to take benefit of compensation granted towards implanting artificial limb and at the same time claim functional disability on the basis of his condition without an artificial limb.
As such, the functional disability of the petitioner upon implanting of artificial limb is likely to be reduced to not more than 40%.
His functional disability is accordingly taken as 40%.

Since the date of birth of the petitioner as per his Aadhar card, is 10.02.1974, his age at the time of accident on 09.01.2021 would have been 46 years 11 months, for purpose of calculating CHARU GUPTA Date:
